rows.stem:
Consider the following standard electrode potential values :
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}_{(aq)}} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe^{2+}_{(aq)}}\)  \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ} = +\,0.77\) V
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}_{(aq)} + 8\mathrm{H^{+}} + 5\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}_{(aq)}} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O}_{(l)}\)  \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ} = +\,1.51\) V
What is the cell potential for the redox reaction ?
rows.solution:
The cell potential is \(+0{\cdot}74\) V.

Identify the electrodes first. The couple with the HIGHER reduction potential acts as the CATHODE, so permanganate at \(+1{\cdot}51\) V is reduced and the iron couple at \(+0{\cdot}77\) V must be the anode — iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III).

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 1{\cdot}51 - 0{\cdot}77 = +0{\cdot}74\ \mathrm{V}\)

Two traps are built into the options. The value must be POSITIVE for a spontaneous redox reaction, which removes both negative choices. And \(+2{\cdot}28\) is the two potentials ADDED — a common error, since the anode reaction must be REVERSED and its potential subtracted rather than added.

There is a third temptation worth naming: the balanced reaction needs FIVE iron(II) ions per permanganate, so the electron counts differ. Electrode potential is an INTENSIVE property, so it is never multiplied by the number of electrons. Only \(\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = -n\mathrm{F}E^{\circ}\) carries that factor.

rows.subtopic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements
rows.stem: Which of the following ions has the electronic configuration \(\mathrm{3d^6}\) ? (Atomic number : Mn = 25, Co = 27, Ni = 28)

options.label: A
options.text: \(\mathrm{Ni^{3+}}\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\)

options.label: C
options.text: \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\)

rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) has the configuration \(3d^6\).

Build each ion from its atom, remembering that a transition metal loses its \(4s\) electrons FIRST, before any \(3d\).

Cobalt is 27, so the atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^7 4s^2\). Removing three electrons — the two \(4s\) and one \(3d\) — leaves \(3d^6\). That is the answer.

Nickel is 28, \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^8 4s^2\), so \(\mathrm{Ni^{3+}}\) is \(3d^7\).
Manganese is 25, \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\), so \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\) and \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is \(3d^4\).

The shortcut is to subtract the charge from the atomic number and then fill up to argon's 18: cobalt's \(27 - 3 = 24\) electrons leave \(24 - 18 = 6\) in the \(3d\) set.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Which of the following aqueous solution will have highest boiling point ?

options.label: A
options.text: 1.0 M \(\mathrm{KCl}\)

options.label: B
options.text: 1.0 M \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\)

options.label: C
options.text: 2.0 M \(\mathrm{KCl}\)

options.label: D
options.text: 2.0 M \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\)

rows.solution:
2.0 M POTASSIUM SULPHATE has the highest boiling point.

Elevation of boiling point is a COLLIGATIVE property, so it depends on the number of PARTICLES per litre — the molarity multiplied by the van't Hoff factor.

Potassium chloride gives TWO ions per formula unit, \(i = 2\); potassium sulphate gives THREE, two potassium ions and one sulphate, \(i = 3\).

Multiply out:
1.0 M \(\mathrm{KCl}\) gives \(1 \times 2 = 2\)
1.0 M \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) gives \(1 \times 3 = 3\)
2.0 M \(\mathrm{KCl}\) gives \(2 \times 2 = 4\)
2.0 M \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) gives \(2 \times 3 = 6\)

The last is the largest, so that solution boils highest. Neither concentration alone decides it — the two 2.0 M solutions differ, and so do the two sulphate solutions — which is why both factors must be multiplied together.

rows.stem: Amides can be converted into amines by the reaction named

options.label: A
options.text: Hoffmann degradation

options.label: B
options.text: Ammonolysis

options.label: C
options.text: Carbylamine

options.label: D
options.text: Diazotisation

rows.solution:
The reaction is HOFFMANN DEGRADATION, also written Hofmann bromamide degradation.

An amide treated with bromine and aqueous alkali gives a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{R{-}CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The lost carbon is the CARBONYL carbon, which leaves as carbonate, and the alkyl group migrates from that carbon to the nitrogen.

Its value is that it gives a PURE PRIMARY amine, uncontaminated by secondary or tertiary product, and it works for aromatic amides as well.

The other three do different things. Ammonolysis makes amines from alkyl halides and ammonia, and gives a mixture. The carbylamine reaction TESTS for a primary amine rather than making one. Diazotisation converts a primary amine into a diazonium salt, which is the opposite direction.

rows.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about glucose ?

options.label: A
options.text: It is an aldohexose.

options.label: B
options.text: On heating with HI it forms n-hexane.

options.label: C
options.text: It is present in pyranose form.

options.label: D
options.text: It gives 2, 4 DNP test.

rows.solution:
The false statement is that glucose gives the 2,4-DNP test.

Glucose does NOT respond to the characteristic carbonyl tests — it gives no 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone, no addition product with sodium bisulphite, and no colour with Schiff's reagent.

The reason is that glucose exists almost entirely in its CYCLIC hemiacetal form, in which the aldehyde group is not present as such. Only a trace of the open chain form is available at any moment, and these reagents are not powerful enough to pull the equilibrium across.

That was one of the observations that forced the cyclic structure on chemists, since the other evidence pointed to an aldehyde.

The three true statements are all standard. Glucose is an ALDOHEXOSE, six carbons with an aldehyde group. Heating with hydroiodic acid and red phosphorus gives N-HEXANE, proving the straight chain. And it exists in the PYRANOSE form, a six-membered ring.

Note that glucose DOES reduce Tollens' and Fehling's reagents, which are alkaline and do shift the equilibrium.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Vitamin C cannot be stored in our body.
Reason (R) : Vitamin C is fat soluble and is excreted from the body in urine.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Vitamin C genuinely cannot be stored in the body, which is why it must be supplied regularly and why a few weeks without fresh fruit brings on scurvy.

But the Reason has the SOLUBILITY wrong. Vitamin C is WATER SOLUBLE, not fat soluble — that is precisely the property the Assertion depends on.

The Reason is also self-contradictory. A FAT soluble vitamin is stored in the liver and in adipose tissue and is NOT excreted in the urine; excretion in urine is what happens to a water soluble one. So the second half of the Reason describes water solubility while the first half claims fat solubility.

Corrected to "water soluble", the Reason would have explained the Assertion exactly: dissolving in the body's aqueous fluids means any excess passes out in the urine and no reserve accumulates. The same holds for the B group; vitamins A, D, E and K are the fat soluble ones, and those ARE stored.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The half life of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of the reactant is reduced to one half of its initial concentration.
Reason (R) : In first order kinetics when concentration of reactant is doubled, its half life is doubled.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

The Assertion states the DEFINITION of half-life correctly, and it applies to a reaction of any order.

The Reason is wrong for FIRST order kinetics. There the half-life is entirely INDEPENDENT of the initial concentration:
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\)

No concentration term appears, so doubling the starting amount leaves the half-life unchanged. This is why radioactive decay, which is first order, has a fixed half-life whatever the size of the sample.

The claim in the Reason would be true of a ZERO order reaction, where \(t_{1/2} = [\mathrm{R}]_0/2k\) and the half-life is proportional to the starting concentration — the Reason has attached zero order behaviour to first order kinetics.

For second order the half-life would be HALVED instead, being inversely proportional to the starting concentration.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Bromination of benzoic acid gives m-bromobenzoic acid.
Reason (R) : Carboxyl group increases the electron density at the meta position.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Bromination of benzoic acid does give mainly the META product, so the Assertion holds. The carboxyl group is a meta directing substituent.

But the Reason has the mechanism backwards. The carboxyl group WITHDRAWS electron density from the ring, both inductively and by resonance — it does not increase it anywhere.

Meta substitution arises from a comparison of shortfalls, not from an increase. Attack at the ortho or para position gives an intermediate carbocation with positive charge on the very carbon bearing the electron-withdrawing group, which is strongly destabilising. Attack at META avoids that, so the meta intermediate is the LEAST unstable of the three, and substitution goes there.

The overall effect is still DEACTIVATION: benzoic acid brominates more slowly than benzene does, not faster. A group that genuinely raised the electron density would speed the reaction up and direct ortho, para, as \(-\mathrm{OH}\) and \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) do.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : EDTA is a hexadentate ligand.
Reason (R) : EDTA has 2 nitrogen and 4 oxygen donor atoms.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

DENTICITY counts the donor atoms through which a ligand binds the metal, so listing those atoms is exactly what establishes the claim.

The ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion has four \(-\mathrm{CH_2COO^-}\) arms attached to a \(-\mathrm{CH_2CH_2}-\) bridge between two nitrogens. That gives TWO nitrogen donors and FOUR carboxylate oxygen donors — six in all, which is what HEXADENTATE means.

Six donors is exactly what an octahedral centre requires, so a single EDTA ion can wrap right around the metal, closing five chelate rings in the process.

The grip is correspondingly strong, and that is what EDTA is used for: softening hard water by holding calcium and magnesium, treating lead poisoning, and as the standard reagent in complexometric titrations.

rows.stem:
Write equations for the following :
(a) Oxidation of chloroform by air and light
(b) Reaction of chlorobenzene with \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\) / anhyd. \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Chloroform is slowly OXIDISED by air in the presence of light to PHOSGENE, a highly poisonous gas:
\(2\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\mathrm{COCl_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl}\)

This is why chloroform is stored in DARK coloured bottles, kept full and tightly closed so that little air remains, with a little ethanol added to destroy any phosgene that does form.

(b) Chloromethane with anhydrous aluminium chloride is a FRIEDEL-CRAFTS ALKYLATION. The chlorine already on the ring is DEACTIVATING, withdrawing density inductively, but ORTHO, PARA DIRECTING, because its lone pair is donated into the ring by resonance:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{o\text{-}}\ \text{and}\ \mathrm{p\text{-}ClC_6H_4CH_3} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The products are 2-CHLOROTOLUENE and 4-CHLOROTOLUENE, the para isomer predominating because the ortho position is crowded by the chlorine already there. The catalyst must be ANHYDROUS — moisture destroys it.

rows.stem: Give the reaction of glucose with acetic anhydride. Presence of which group is confirmed by this reaction ?
rows.solution:
Acetic anhydride acetylates every hydroxyl group in the glucose molecule:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} + 5(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_7O(OCOCH_3)_5} + 5\,\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

The product is GLUCOSE PENTA-ACETATE.

The reaction confirms the presence of FIVE HYDROXYL GROUPS. Counting the acetyl groups introduced counts the hydroxyls that were there, since each ester formed consumed exactly one.

Two further conclusions were drawn from it historically. Because all five acetylate readily and none resists, none of them can be attached to the same carbon as another — two hydroxyls on one carbon would form an unstable arrangement — so the five are on five DIFFERENT carbons.

And the penta-acetate does NOT react with hydroxylamine, which showed that glucose has no free aldehyde group once all its hydroxyls are locked: the fifth acetyl has closed off the anomeric hydroxyl and the ring can no longer open.

rows.stem:
(a) On the basis of crystal field theory write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^5}\) ion with a weak ligand for which \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\).
(b) Explain \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) is an inner orbital complex whereas \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\) is an outer orbital complex.
[Atomic number : Fe = 26]
rows.solution:
(a) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^2\).

In an octahedral field the d orbitals split into a lower set of three, \(t_{2g}\), and an upper set of two, \(e_g\), separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron entering chooses between two costs: promotion to the upper set costs \(\Delta_0\), while pairing in the lower set costs the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

The question specifies \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) — a WEAK FIELD — so promotion is the cheaper option and the electrons spread out as widely as they can, one to each of the five orbitals.

All FIVE are unpaired, so this is a HIGH SPIN complex with the maximum possible magnetic moment, \(\mu = \sqrt{5 \times 7} = 5{\cdot}92\) B.M.

A STRONG field would have given \(t_{2g}^5\,e_g^0\) instead — one unpaired electron and \(\mu = 1{\cdot}73\) B.M. The same \(d^5\) ion gives opposite magnetic behaviour depending only on the ligand, which is why measuring the moment identifies the field strength.

(b) Because CYANIDE is a STRONG field ligand and FLUORIDE a WEAK one, and only a strong field frees an inner d orbital.

Iron is \(+3\) in both, so both have \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} = 3d^5\) — five orbitals, one electron each to begin with.

In \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) cyanide forces those five electrons to pair into the lower three orbitals as \(t_{2g}^5\). That leaves TWO INNER \(3d\) orbitals empty, which with the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) give \(d^2sp^3\) — an INNER ORBITAL complex, with one unpaired electron.

In \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\) fluoride cannot force any pairing, so all five \(3d\) orbitals stay singly occupied and NONE is available. Bonding must reach OUTWARDS to the \(4d\) set, giving \(sp^3d^2\) — an OUTER ORBITAL complex, with five unpaired electrons.

The magnetic moments distinguish them at once: 1.73 B.M. against 5.92 B.M.

rows.stem:
(i) Give a chemical test to distinguish between ethanal and ethanoic acid.
(ii) Why is the \(\alpha\)-hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic in nature ?
(iii) An organic compound 'A' with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}\) undergoes acid hydrolysis to form two compounds 'B' and 'C'. Oxidation of 'C' with acidified potassium permanganate also produces 'B'. Sodium salt of 'B' on heating with soda lime gives methane.
(1) Identify 'A', 'B' and 'C'.
(2) Out of 'B' and 'C', which will have higher boiling point ? Give reason.
rows.solution:
(i) Add SODIUM HYDROGENCARBONATE solution to each. ETHANOIC ACID gives brisk EFFERVESCENCE of carbon dioxide, being acidic enough to displace it from the salt; ETHANAL gives no reaction at all:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{NaHCO_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COONa} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow\)

Tollens' reagent serves in the opposite direction: warmed with ethanal it gives a SILVER MIRROR, the aldehyde being oxidised to the acid, while ethanoic acid gives nothing, being already at that oxidation level.

(ii) Because the CARBANION left behind is stabilised by RESONANCE with the carbonyl group.

Removing an \(\alpha\) hydrogen leaves a negative charge on the carbon next to the carbonyl, and that charge does not stay there — it is delocalised onto the OXYGEN, which is far better able to carry it:
\(\mathrm{{}^-CH_2{-}CH{=}O} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}O^-}\)

The resulting ENOLATE is stable enough for a base to remove the hydrogen, which it could never do from an ordinary alkane. This acidity is what makes the aldol condensation and \(\alpha\)-halogenation possible.

(iii)(1) Work backwards from the last clue. A sodium salt heated with soda lime loses carbon dioxide and gives the hydrocarbon with ONE CARBON FEWER, so a salt giving METHANE came from a TWO-carbon acid:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), ethanoic acid

Oxidation of C gives B, and an alcohol oxidises to the acid with the same carbon count:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), ethanol

Acid hydrolysis of an ESTER gives an acid and an alcohol, and \(\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}\) is exactly the ester of these two:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5}\), ethyl ethanoate

(2) ETHANOIC ACID has the higher boiling point — 391 K against ethanol's 351 K.

Both form hydrogen bonds, but the acid forms TWO between each pair of molecules, its carboxyl groups locking together into a DIMER through an eight-membered ring. Ethanol has only one \(\mathrm{O-H}\) per molecule and forms an open chain rather than a closed pair, so its association is the weaker.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(a) A transition element X has electronic configuration [Ar] \(\mathrm{4s^2\ 3d^3}\). Predict its likely oxidation states.
(b) Complete the reaction mentioning all the products formed :
\(2\,\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta}\)
(c) Account for the following :
(i) In the 3d transition series, zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation.
(ii) \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) ion is unstable in aqueous solution.
(iii) Actinoids show more number of oxidation states than lanthanoids.
rows.solution:
(a) The element is VANADIUM, since \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,4s^2 3d^3\) accounts for 23 electrons.

The states available run from the lowest, using the \(4s\) pair alone, up to the highest, using every \(4s\) electron and every UNPAIRED \(3d\) electron:
\(+2\), \(+3\), \(+4\) and \(+5\)

The maximum is \(2 + 3 = 5\), and vanadium does reach it, in the vanadate ion — which equals its GROUP NUMBER, as it does for chromium and manganese further along.

The higher states survive only in combination with OXYGEN or FLUORINE, small and strongly electronegative; \(+4\) and \(+5\) are the commonly encountered ones, and \(+2\) is a strong reducing agent.

(b) Potassium permanganate decomposes on heating, manganese ending in TWO different oxidation states:
\(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

The products are POTASSIUM MANGANATE, MANGANESE DIOXIDE and OXYGEN. Manganese falls from \(+7\) to \(+6\) in one product and to \(+4\) in the other, while oxygen rises from \(-2\) to 0 — so this is the decomposition that makes solid permanganate a source of oxygen in the laboratory.

(c)(i) Because zinc has a COMPLETELY FILLED \(3d\) subshell, so its d electrons take no part in metallic bonding.

The strength of the metallic bond across the series depends on how many UNPAIRED d electrons each atom contributes to it. Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\) — every d electron paired and held tightly to its own atom — so only the two \(4s\) electrons are available.

With the weakest metallic bond in the series, zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation, and the lowest melting and boiling points; mercury below it is liquid at room temperature for the same reason.

(ii) Because \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) DISPROPORTIONATES in water:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

The driving force is HYDRATION ENERGY. The \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ion is smaller and doubly charged, so it is hydrated far more strongly than \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) — enough to more than pay for the second ionisation energy.

In the SOLID state, with no water to do the hydrating, copper(I) compounds such as copper(I) chloride and copper(I) iodide are perfectly stable.

(iii) Because in the actinoids the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) orbitals lie CLOSE IN ENERGY, so different numbers of electrons can be used for bonding.

The lanthanoids are dominated by the single state \(+3\), their \(4f\) orbitals being buried deep inside the atom and shielded from any chemical influence.

The \(5f\) orbitals extend much FURTHER OUT, so they are available for bonding rather than inert. Actinoids therefore show \(+3\) through \(+7\) — uranium alone appearing as \(+3\), \(+4\), \(+5\) and \(+6\).
